boundary_rationale: This unit opens the whole triple acrostic at its own tier-1 threshold: the geber's first-person onset is spliced at byte tier as אֲנִ֤י הַגֶּ֨בֶר֙ (oshb:Lam.3.1, byte tier), matched by the WEB witness “I am the man who has seen affliction by the rod of his wrath.” (web:Lam.3.1). The span covers three consecutive triplets of the ch-3 triple acrostic in the witness's own pe-before-ayin order: alef א (3:1-3), bet ב (3:4-6) and gimel ג (3:7-9). Across the nine verses the geber narrates the same first-person register of divine-agency affliction imagery, darkness, a hand turned against him, broken bones, a wall and a chain, a shut prayer, and crooked paths, naming no addressee across the span.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the alef and bet triplets off as a shorter opening unit was considered and rejected because the imprisonment imagery of the gimel triplet continues in the same first-person register, addressed to nobody in particular, just as the triplet before it is.

boundary_rationale: The dalet, he and vav triplets (3:10-12, 3:13-15, 3:16-18) continue the geber's first-person catalogue of affliction under the same voice as the triplets just before them. The unit ends on the starkest line of the whole lament, spliced at byte tier as וְתוֹחַלְתִּ֖י מֵיְהוָֽה (oshb:Lam.3.18, byte tier), rendered inside the WEB witness's own quotation as “My strength has perished, along with my expectation from Yahweh.” (web:Lam.3.18): a declared exhaustion of hope that sets up, but does not itself cross into, the imperative turn of the following verse.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this span through 3:19-21 to include the zayin triplet was considered and rejected because 3:18's declared exhaustion of hope offers a clearer seam for the vav triplet's own close than the imperative onset of 3:19 does.
literature_type_guess: individual complaint catalogue, closing in exhausted hope

boundary_rationale: The zayin, het and tet triplets (3:19-21, 3:22-24, 3:25-27) are held here as the hope-meditation's own opening, though whether the zayin and het triplets (3:19-24) still belong with the preceding catalogue of affliction, or already open the turn to hope, is a genuinely disputed literary question this span discloses rather than resolves. The imperative onset is spliced at byte tier as זְכָר (oshb:Lam.3.19, byte tier), matched by the WEB witness “Remember my affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the bitterness.” (web:Lam.3.19), and the same triplet turns on עַל כֵּ֥ן אוֹחִֽיל (oshb:Lam.3.21, byte tier; WEB “This I recall to my mind; therefore I have hope.”, web:Lam.3.21), the pivot line of the whole chapter. The het triplet names YHWH's hesed, spliced at byte tier as חַֽסְדֵ֤י יְהוָה֙ (oshb:Lam.3.22, byte tier; WEB “It is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.”, web:Lam.3.22), and the tet triplet opens all three of its verses with the same word, tov, meaning good, in immediate succession (sweep: 3 verses), matched by the WEB triad “Yahweh is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.” (web:Lam.3.25), “It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of Yahweh.” (web:Lam.3.26) and “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.” (web:Lam.3.27).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the zayin and het triplets (3:19-24) as the closing unit of the preceding affliction catalogue, rather than the opening of this span, was considered and is recorded as the genuinely disputed alternative, left open rather than settled here.

boundary_rationale: The yod and kaf triplets (3:28-30, 3:31-33) move from a posture of silent submission into an explicit statement of divine compassion; no change of voice or addressee separates them. The kaf triplet opens with a line spliced at byte tier as כִּ֣י לֹ֥א יִזְנַ֛ח לְעוֹלָ֖ם אֲדֹנָֽי (oshb:Lam.3.31, byte tier), rendered by the WEB witness “For the Lord will not cast off forever.” (web:Lam.3.31).

boundary_rationale: The lamed and mem triplets (3:34-36, 3:37-39) turn from the compassion statement to a theodicy reflection argued in the third person about justice and divine sovereignty, staying inside the same wisdom-style register with no first-person geber speech across the six verses. The mem triplet poses two rhetorical questions in succession, the first spliced at byte tier as מִ֣י זֶ֤ה אָמַר֙ וַתֶּ֔הִי אֲדֹנָ֖י לֹ֥א צִוָּֽה (oshb:Lam.3.37, byte tier; WEB “Who is he who says, and it comes to pass, when the Lord doesn’t command it?”, web:Lam.3.37), the second closing the triplet as “Why should a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?” (web:Lam.3.39). This closing question is one candidate hinge into the cohortative confession that opens the next triplet, though whether the turn belongs with the reflection ending here or the confession beginning next is held rather than decided.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this span through the nun triplet (3:40-42) was considered and rejected because the shift from third-person reflection to first-person-plural cohortative confession at 3:40 is a clearer voice-based seam than treating the rhetorical-question close of 3:39 as the boundary by itself.

Labeling this span hope_meditation rather than a bespoke theodicy category is a one-sentence operative-category deviation this span discloses: its content argues justice and sovereignty in the third person rather than continuing the first-person wait-and-hope posture of the triplets just before it, kept here under the same closed vocabulary as the surrounding material.

boundary_rationale: The nun and samekh triplets (3:40-42, 3:43-45) open a first-person-plural confession, spliced at byte tier from its cohortative onset as נַחְפְּשָׂ֤ה דְרָכֵ֨ינוּ֙ וְֽנַחְקֹ֔רָה וְנָשׁ֖וּבָה עַד יְהוָֽה (oshb:Lam.3.40, byte tier), rendered by the WEB witness “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to Yahweh.” (web:Lam.3.40); whether this turn belongs with the reflection ending just before it or with the confession beginning here is held rather than decided. The plural voice continues, spliced at byte tier as נַ֤חְנוּ פָשַׁ֨עְנוּ֙ וּמָרִ֔ינוּ אַתָּ֖ה לֹ֥א סָלָֽחְתָּ (oshb:Lam.3.42, byte tier; WEB “We have transgressed and have rebelled. You have not pardoned.”, web:Lam.3.42), through the first two verses of the pe triplet, which this span closes early: “All our enemies have opened their mouth wide against us.” (web:Lam.3.46) and “Terror and the pit have come on us, devastation and destruction.” (web:Lam.3.47), both still carrying the plural object suffixes. Ending the span at 3:47 cuts inside the pe triplet one verse short of where it closes at Lam.3.48; the SAMEKH inventory there argues mild continuity across the cut, disclosed here rather than treated as a driver, against the tier-1 warrant that follows. The disclosed reason for cutting inside the triplet is the pronoun shift itself: the very next verse turns the plural back to a singular first person, a byte-observable person shift this span treats as the stronger signal over the triplet's own formal boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this span at the pe triplet's own formal boundary (3:48) rather than splitting it after 3:47 was considered and rejected because the plural-to-singular pronoun shift at 3:48 is a clearer tier-1 signal than the triplet's own tier-3 parashah-mark symmetry.

boundary_rationale: The qof and resh triplets (3:55-57, 3:58-60) turn the geber's first-person report into direct second-person address to YHWH, spliced at byte tier from its opening invocation as קָרָ֤אתִי שִׁמְךָ֙ יְהוָ֔ה מִבּ֖וֹר תַּחְתִּיּֽוֹת (oshb:Lam.3.55, byte tier), matched by the WEB witness “I called on your name, Yahweh, out of the lowest dungeon.” (web:Lam.3.55). The qof triplet closes with reported reassurance, spliced at byte tier as קָרַ֨בְתָּ֙ בְּי֣וֹם אֶקְרָאֶ֔ךָּ אָמַ֖רְתָּ אַל תִּירָֽא (oshb:Lam.3.57, byte tier), whose own nested quotation the WEB witness renders “Don’t be afraid.” (web:Lam.3.57), and the resh triplet opens under the Adonai title, spliced at byte tier as רַ֧בְתָּ אֲדֹנָ֛י רִיבֵ֥י נַפְשִׁ֖י גָּאַ֥לְתָּ חַיָּֽי (oshb:Lam.3.58, byte tier; WEB “Lord, you have pleaded the causes of my soul. You have redeemed my life.”, web:Lam.3.58), before turning to report the enemies' plotting under the YHWH name again in its closing two verses.

boundary_rationale: The shin and tav triplets (3:61-63, 3:64-66) close the whole triple acrostic, still reporting the enemies' plotting under direct address to YHWH through 3:63 before turning, in the tav triplet, to a threefold imperative-future imprecation against them, each verse-initial in the same construction (sweep: 3 verses): תָּשִׁ֨יב לָהֶ֥ם גְּמ֛וּל יְהוָ֖ה כְּמַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יְדֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Lam.3.64, byte tier), תִּתֵּ֤ן לָהֶם֙ מְגִנַּת לֵ֔ב תַּאֲלָֽתְךָ֖ לָהֶֽם (oshb:Lam.3.65, byte tier) and תִּרְדֹּ֤ף בְּאַף֙ וְתַשְׁמִידֵ֔ם מִתַּ֖חַת שְׁמֵ֥י יְהוָֽה (oshb:Lam.3.66, byte tier); the WEB witness renders the opening verb “You will pay them back, Yahweh, according to the work of their hands.” (web:Lam.3.64) and the closing verb, at the poem's own final verse, “You will pursue them in anger, and destroy them from under the heavens of Yahweh.” (web:Lam.3.66). This closing shift from petition-report to imperative imprecation is the disclosed reason the span is not extended further back into the qof/resh material; it is an operative-category deviation from a plain unit_type label, disclosed here rather than left silent.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this span back to include the qof and resh material was considered and rejected because the shift from petition-report to imperative imprecation beginning at 3:64 is a discourse-frame change distinct enough to mark its own closing unit.
